label: text
text: Rochampton will lose the entry of 8: MJ Jacob, the present covered co-t champion. The Lawn Tennis Association have suspended Line from tournament competition in this country until further notice. A notification to that effect was conveyed to the executive at Roehampton. Mr. Jacob, who was on the ground, had not received personal notification of this decree. Mr. Jacob's suspension is the outcome of a breach of the amateur rule which apparently unwittingly he committed by joining a London team visiting Paris as far back as November last. The captain of this team had failed to obtain the necessary sanction from the Lawn Tennis Association, and his team accepted expenses from the Paris club, not only for their match, but for a subsequent tournament held on the same courts. This was contrary to the regulations; the offence has been admitted; it became a question of inflicting a penalty. The council suspended the captain of the team for twelve months. The other members were advised that they must agree to refund the proportion of their expenses paid by their hosts.

label: text
text: The negotiations were long. The I.T.A. claim that they have shown both justice and patience. I do not think that can be disputed. Yesterday's action against Mr. Jacob was taken, not, as I understand, because he disputed the commission of a technical offence; he held that his own association, the Association of All India, should be consulted as to the validity of the verdict. In other words, he wanted to appeal to another court. The I.T.A. claimed that they, and they alone, had jurisdiction in this matter, since Jacob proposed to play at their own tournaments, and he had admittedly (though not necessarily consciously) broken one of their regulations. They are unquestionably right. But I hope a way out will be found, and that Jacob's suspension may be withdrawn at the earliest possible moment. He has committed no offence which cannot be condoned by a frank admission of error. Nor are the council such "tyrants" that they would wish to deprive a former Davis Cup captain, who has taken up his residence in this country, of his desire to compete in our tournament, always provided their authority is admitted. I think that is essential for all players who compete in tournaments held under the sanction of the association. I would add that I found no evidence in support of the report published that the competitors at Roehampton were anxious to withdraw their entries in protest of the official action. A certain measure of sympathy was naturally expressed for Mr. Jacob, but it was felt that the matter was personal one between himself and the governing body. [Subsequently, Reuter, cabled that Jacob's and Fyzee's suspensions were withdrawn.]

label: paragraph_title
text: SERGT. W. ALJEN'S RETIREMENT.

label: text
text:
A record of 33 years' service in the Colony will be left behind by Sergt. W. Allen of the Royal Naval Yard Police who sails for Home by the s.s. Carmarthenshire on June 11. His many friends will regret the loss of such a generous, genial personality, also that his departure has been necessitated by ill-health.
Sergt. Allen had been connected with the Royal Naval Yard Police in Hongkong for sixteen years and prior to that laid served over sixteen years here with the Royal Garrison Artillery. Before coming to Hongkong he had seen service at Gibraltar, Aden and India.

label: text
text: Many residents will best remember Sergt. Allen because of his association with the boxing tournaments held in the City Hall in connection with the arranging of which he was valued helper. It was seldom that he was not to be seen at the ringside at these tournaments.

label: paragraph_title
text: Local Honours.

label: text
text: To the Editor of the China Mail?

label: text
text: Sir.—The Hongkong's Honours list, is sadly akin to what the prevailing note in feminine fashions is said to be—slim. Does it tell us, in the words of Mr. Arnold Bennett "how the Government feels in its inside"—assuming that recommendations for Honours are made by the Government? Mr. Tanner gets an I.S.O. In addition to that well-merited recognition he is to be congratulated on the length of quiet but effective service he has been able to do in an exacting profession. For the rest—social workers, philantropists, commercial magnates, Government servants, and the people who do things and, blush to find themselves famous must wait. The Government "in its inside" feels that no one as yet has reached maturity. In Malaya they do these things differently. The Government's "inside" there is less liverish. It sees not as through a glass darkly. My fear is that this fact being known the exodus of the classes we have mentioned will become great; we shall have no reformers, no workers for good; no philantropists left to do the good things that find their own reward, which perhaps will be just as well. The bestowing of honours is perhaps veiled in mystery. Doubtless they were first given for doughty deeds. Up to quite recently they were also bestowed for "dough" by deeds; but they have been known to be given for services rendered by those with sufficient time on their hands. The system generally has been wrong—so much so that quite respectable gentlemen in such enlightened places as South Africa and Australia have definitely decided to refuse all honours. I have an open mind on the question. If anything I would do away with the system entirely unless the holders of Honours undertook to remain here all their lives. In its place I would have a temple of fame—something on the lines of the Temple of the 500 Geneii at Canton—wherein Tussaud-like representations of all those who have served the Colony well would be permanently housed. Here on at least one day in the year I would bring the school children of the place to rest their eyes and minds on the effigies of those who had done so much for so little without impairing their health. And any who called this the Hall of Pomposity would receive my severest rebuke. But after all I am of Cato's mind when he said: I had rather it should be asked why I had not a statue than why I had one.

label: text

label: text
text: YESTERDAY'S RECEPTION

label: text
text: Operated by the Dollar Line free from the Shipping Board control, the s.s. President Polk could carry whatever-drinks the passengers might desire, but in accordance with the principles of the owners she is "dry" from choice.

label: text
text: As she lay at the wharf on the Kowloon side yesterday this liner was boarded by those interested in passenger traffic and in the local shipping world generally. The many improvements which have been effected on the ship since it was last in port were the subject of much comment.

label: text
text: Advantage has been taken of the opportunity afforded by the burning out of the boat at the disastrous fire at the New York wharves to re-model it entirely and this is particularly noticeable in regard to the utilising of space which had been devoted to hatchways for such purposes as a social hall, increased deck facilities and other comforts for the passengers, there being much increased accommodation.

label: text
text: As an all-round the-world-liner the President Polk has to be prepared for anything in the way of weather and this difficult problem has been met by the installation in the suite of radiators side by side with shower boths and all the cooling devices which the ingenuity of man can devise. All the cabins are roomy and fitted up with the latest improvements—mirrors at the back of cabin and cupboard doors being particularly of note. Everywhere there are odd corners where taps obligingly provide iced water aplenty. Again, there are covered walks for use in cold weather and plenty of open walking space when passengers experience such weather as Hongkong is providing them with at present. Everywhere there are ingeniously operated skylights which indicate the provision of supplies of cool and fresh air at the passengers' convenience.

label: text
text: Amongst those who yesterday afternoon made the acquaintance of the new ship and of Capt. Ahlin Mr. Charman, the purser, and Mr. E. L. label: text
text: Impressions of Edinburgh are given in the "Scotland To-day" series in the "Observer." The citizen," says the writer, "is an abridgment of all that is steady, regular, proper, and persistent," and he has an interesting theory on how Edinburgh's beauty and tradition affects the character.

label: text
text: That is: Edinburgh all over—handling monduities with a touch of patronage, serenely confident in her own instinct and tradition.

label: text
text: Edinburgh is as sure of herself as Paris, to whose beauty, her own has some cousinship. Both are externally cities of pleasure, proud in their pattern, haunted by history. Both have developed by survivorship a firm strain of humanity which takes a fine polish.

label: paragraph_title
text: A KINDER PEOPLE

label: text
text: But the war and all that it set in train have "softened". Edinburgh where it needed softening. It was not the most human of entities when I "knew it" immediately: "after the spacious times of Lord Neaves and Lord Deaves."

label: text
text: That seems to have gone, leaving a kin or place, and people. There may be: "win-wealth" in Edinburgh, but there is more war-lovers. Simpler living has evoked more of the simpler graces to sweeten it.

label: text
text: Edinburgh is not so chic as of old, and one misses the fine edge that used to gleams on its formalities. But it is replaced by a tenner humbism, mellower on the surface and more active-minded within.

label: text
text: Here (as in Aberdeen) the new type of educated young woman is a conspicuous and engaging figure. Her growing sense of solidarity with all working women thaws much class-consciousness. Tonic and exacting, explicit and confident, she is, like the young Victoria, "re-resolute little tit"; full of intelligent curiosities: forthright though not bold; by no means idolatrous of the male kind; but still not evolving towards sexlessness; capable of keeping fashion in its place.

label: text
text: CHUROH-GOING DIMINISTHING.

label: text
text: Some changes move slowly; church-going diminishes; and the wireless on Sunday seems to prove further welcome. Public golf courses are closed on the first day of the week, and though private ones are busy, I am not sure that a young advocate on his manifest way to a game feels quite undisturbed in meeting a Judge. Lawn tennis, with its unsabbatary, can tempo, is the preserve of the iconoclast. The motorist betakes himself to "Peebles for pleasure."

label: text
text: For the rest there is a certain amount of inevitable loafing; but, of course, there are worse places than Edinburgh to load in, for its reveries are endless.

label: text
text: On week-days Princes Street is, as ever, the most inspiring of parades. The interior of Parliament House suggests the glamour of a great profession with more concentration than the Strand Law Courts.

label: text
text: The student's hive beyond the Meadows should find its poet some day. The pursuit of education is the stimulus to much of the Pluck that labels Edinburgh to day more accurately than her traditional "Pride and Poverty."

label: text
text: Her poor, like her antiquities, are well cared for: on the one hand, it is no secret that some of her fine libraries are not exactly in the best of order.

label: text
text: It remains a complex city, of various, and only slightly overlapping; circles. And, beneath them all, the old Edinburgh bohemianism (persistent from the days of Ferguson and long before, always retiring, and now more deeply hidden than ever) still chuckles in its caverns to those who have a yielding ear.

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text: A ruthless examination of some weather proverbs from the scientific points of view formed part of a highly technical paper on "Clouds and weather forecasting" at the meeting held to celebrate the seventy-fifth anniversary of the Royal Meteorological Society. It was read by Dr. E. van Everdingen, the head of the Dutch Meteorological Service.

label: text
text: "The weather wisdom of the man in the "street," said Dr. van Everdingen, "especially in the streets of London is rather limited. The man in the field who consults the look of the sky may at times be more successful in short-range forecasting than the professional meteorologist, but whether forecasting in his hands is more of an art than a science."
